# A Simple Circuit for Time-Resolved Luminescence (TRL) Measurement Instruments: Demonstration Through a Smartphone-Based TRL Imager for Anticounterfeiting Application

**Authors:** Alim Gulbag; Michael Huang; Brian Rong; Benjamin Sreenan; Xiaoshan Zhu

**Affiliations:** Department of Electrical and Biomedical Engineering, University of Nevada Reno, NV 98557 USA

## Abstract

Time-resolved luminescence (TRL) measurement is a sensitive detection technique by eliminating sample autofluorescence, but TRL measurement instruments composed of multiple key components (e.g., a rapidly pulsed light excitation source, a time-gated optical detector, and a synchronization module aligning the timing between the light source and the detector) have been sophisticated, expensive, or bulky, which limits their point-of-care or in-field applications. To reduce the cost and complexity of these instruments, in this work, we developed a simple circuit for rapid LED pulsing and accurate timing synchronization, and implemented it in a compact TRL imager with a UV LED as light source and a chopper-coupled smartphone camera as time-gated optical detector. The TRL measurement of this imager using this circuit was successfully validated through an anticounterfeiting application. We believe that this simple circuit can be adopted in the development of low-cost and compact TRL measurement instruments for broad point-of-care or in-field applications.

## INTRODUCTION

Time-resolved luminescence (TRL) measurement, utilizing long-lived-luminescence materials (e.g., lanthanide-based complexes, manganese (Mn)-doped nanocrystals), is a sensitive detection technique [1]. In this technique, after pulsed excitation, sample autofluorescence decays within tens of nanoseconds, but these materials still emit long-lasting luminescence for signal measurement. Due to its high signal-to-background (S/B) ratio, this technique has gained wide applications in anticounterfeiting, sensing, and imaging [1–2]. Despite its effectiveness in sensitive detection, the instruments for TRL measurement are generally complex involving multiple components (e.g., a rapidly pulsed light excitation source, a high-speed time-gated optical detector, and a synchronization module aligning the timing between the light source and the detector) [2]. Moreover, some components such as photodetectors and synchronization modules are expensive or bulky. As a result, large, complicated, and costly instruments usually are developed for laboratory use, and the point-of-care or in-field applications of TRL measurement have been limited. With the recent technology advance in light excitation sources (e.g., high-power UV LEDs), mechanical chopper-based optical detector, and manufacturing, compact instruments have been reported [3–4]. But electronic circuits for timing synchronization as well as light source pulsing were still sophisticated in these systems. For instance, these systems used either a digital delay generator (e.g., DG535, > $4,000, Stanford Research System) or FGPA/MCU programming for synchronization and light pulsing, which are expensive, or complex/time-consuming in development. To develop low-cost and miniaturized TRL instruments for potential point-of-care or in-field applications, simple, cheap, and compact circuits are highly needed.

In this work, we developed a simple circuit using dual retriggerable monostable multivibrators and several additional components for timing synchronization and LED pulsing, which costs less than $40 and is easy to tune. We implemented this circuit in a compact TRL imager with a UV LED (up to 1 W optical output power) as light source and a chopper-coupled smartphone camera as time-gated optical detector. Using Mn-doped nanocrystals (NCs) as long-lived-luminescence materials (luminescence lifetime at ~ 2 ms) [5], we demonstrated that this imager using this circuit functioned properly for its TRL measurement in an anticounterfeiting application. We believe that this simple circuit can be adopted in the development of low-cost and compact TRL measurement instruments using materials with luminescence lifetimes at milli-second levels for broad point-of-care or in-field applications.

## EXPERIMENTAL

### Materials and Apparatus

A mechanical optical chopper with a controller (MC2000B) was from Thorlabs. LEDs (ELUA3535NU3, ~ 400 nm emission, 1 W optical output), dual retriggerable monostable multivibrators (SN74AHC123AN), and other electronics parts were from Digikey or Mouser. A smartphone (iPhone 15) was from Apple. Adhesive films were from USA Scientific. Organic solvent Tetrahydrofuran (THF) and glass slides were from VWR. Mn-doped and undoped NCs (Mn:AgZnInS/ZnS and AgZnInS/ZnS NCs) were prepared using a previous method [5]. All mechanical parts were prepared through 3D printing. Oscilloscope Tektronix TDS-2012B 100 MHZ and Hamamatsu photomultiplier tube (PMT) H10721–20 with related components were used in experiments for circuit characterization. Image J, an open-source image processing program developed at the National Institutes of Health, was used for image analysis.

### Imaging Experiments and Image Analysis

After an adhesive film was cut with 2-mm through-holes using laser, it adhered to a glass slide. Then, 3 μL of Mn-doped NCs dissolved in THF with a concentration (e.g., 100 μg/mL) was pipetted to a through-hole or a well. After THF evaporated, the adhesive film was peeled off, and a spot of Mn-doped NCs was deposited on the glass slide for TRL measurement. Each testing condition was repeated in triplicates. For anticounterfeiting application, an array of 2 × 3 through-holes on a glass slide were deposited with undoped NCs (1 mg/mL, luminescence lifetime < 1 μs) and then some selected through-holes (or wells) were further deposited with Mn-doped NCs. After dry and film peel-off, the glass slide was imaged under time-resolved mode and non-time-resolved mode. For image analysis, we took multiple images for each testing condition. For the region of interests (i.e., NC-deposited spot) in the images, we used Z-stack to get the Z-stack mean of all images and then averaged all these values to achieve a new mean value with a standard deviation. The reason to use Z-stack is that NCs are not evenly distributed in each well due to solvent surface tension during THF evaporation. Triplicate averaging produced a final average with a standard deviation. The S/B ratio was calculated as the ratio between the mean value for a certain Mn-doped NC concentration and the mean value for a blank glass. No additional processes like brightness or contrast enhancement were applied to the images, considering possible in-field applications.

## RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

### Overview of TRL, the Circuit, and the TRL Imager

TRL measurement using a pulsed LED excitation source and an optical chopper-based camera has two basic steps, as shown in Fig. 1(A). First, LED is turned on for sample excitation. In the excitation phase, Mn-doped NCs and sample matrix will produce signal and background, respectively. But the camera will be blocked by the chopper blade, and no signal and background can be read by camera. Second, after LED is turned off, with a certain time delay, sample autofluorescence fades out quickly due to its short lifetime, but Mn-doped NCs still emit the signal due to their long luminescence lifetime at ~ 2 ms. Then, the chopper blade is rotated away or opened, so that the camera records the signal only. TRL measurement thus naturally has a high S/B ratio. In this system, the chopper is controlled by a controller which also provides a reference-output (a frequency clock aligned with the rotation speed of chopper). To ensure TRL measurement, the timing synchronization between the pulsed LED and the chopper reference-output is critical and needs to be manually tuned, so that no excitation light leak from the LED into the camera. It is noted that the camera blocking/opening status is not exactly aligned with the falling or rising edge of the chopper reference-output due to the size of pinhole for camera recording, the positioning between the camera and the chopper, and so on [3]. In other words, at the falling edge of the chopper reference-output, the camera could be blocked or opened. For such uncertain circumstances, Fig. 1(B) illustrates our proposed method for timing synchronization – the falling edge of the chopper reference-output triggers a tunable pulse (defined as the delay pulse (Pdelay)), and the falling edge of the delay pulse then triggers another tunable pulse (defined as the LED pulse) to turn on LED with a certain pulsing width (Pwidth). If the camera is opened at the falling edge of the chopper reference-output, Pdelay can be tuned long enough until the camera is blocked and then LED is triggered to turn on for excitation. After LED is on, Pwidth of LED should be tuned in an appropriate range to avoid LED light leaking into the camera (i.e., LED should be turned off before the camera is opened again). Oppositely, if the camera is blocked at the falling edge of the chopper reference-output, Pdelay can be set at its minimum value, and Pwidth of LED is thus tuned in an appropriate range for excitation.

Different from conventional digital delay generators or FPGA/MCU programming for timing synchronization and LED pulsing, our circuit simply uses low-cost dual retriggerable monostable multivibrators and several additional components, and its schematic is presented in Fig. 1(C). With a multivibrator, the falling edge of the chopper reference-output is used to trigger a pulse (the delay pulse in Fig. 1(B)). With another multivibrator, the falling edge of the delay pulse is used to trigger another pulse (the LED pulse in Figure 1(B)). The pulse time (Pdelay) of the delay pulse and the pulse time (Pwidth) of the LED pulse are determined by a pair of external potentiometers and capacitors, allowing for fine tuning of output durations (τ = R × C). Potentiometers and capacitors were selected in this work to tune these two time-parameters in the range of 10 μs to 2 ms. Appropriate components can be chosen for broader time tuning, depending on specific applications. In this circuit, the LED pulse is fed into a LED driver to rapidly pulse a UV LED. The LED driver essentially is an inverter (a pair of NMOSFET and PMOSFET) with LED as load. The NMOS (IRF540) and PMOS (IRF9Z34N) pair works like a conventional CMOS inverter in a push-pull mode to turn on and off LED, respectively. Note that both MOSFETs are of high-speeds (< 55 ns turn on/off dynamic times) and low turn-on resistances (~ 0.1 ohms), which will facilitate the rapid pulsing of LED. A 5.6 ohms resistor is connected between the drain of PMOS and the drain of NMOS (or the LED anode), which is used to set the LED turn-on current at ~ 200 mA for ~ 200 mW optical output and also limit the transient current from power supply to ground through two MOSFETs during switching.

Fig. 1(D) shows the implementation of this circuit into a compact TRL imager with a chopper-based smartphone and a UV LED. 3D printing was used for the preparation of all other parts.

### Circuit Characterization

Fig. 2(A) shows the timing demonstration of the dual multivibrators with the chopper reference-output as the input and the delay pulse and the LED pulse as the outputs. In this demonstration, at the falling edge of the chopper reference-output, the delay pulse goes high and lasts for 10μs (Pdelay). At the falling edge of the delay pulse, the LED pulse goes high for 1.9 ms (Pwidth) and turns off before the chopper reference-output goes high. Both Pdelay and Pwidth can be further tuned to different values through the potentiometers.

To test the light switching dynamics of LED and the LED light-output stability over continuous pulsing through the LED driver, a PMT H10721–20 was used to detect the light dynamics and intensity of LED [6]. Fig. 2(B–C) show the rising and falling dynamics of the light from LED with an electrical turn-on or -off control. The rising time and the rising delay time are 0.16 μs and 0.51 μs, respectively. The falling time and the falling delay time are 0.34 μs and 1.23 μs, respectively. Fig. 2(D) shows the normalized LED output-light stability over four hours under different pulsing conditions (250, 500, and 1000 kHz with 50% duty cycles). Each data point in Fig. 2(D) has a relative standard deviation less than 0.03%. Under each testing condition, the relative signal variation over time is no more than 0.08%. No obvious photobleaching of Mn-doped NCs was observed for all tested LED pulsing conditions. From the LED testing data, it can be concluded that the LED driver is able to turn LED on or off fast enough and thus do not affect the chopper-based smartphone to capture the Mn-doped NC luminescence (lasting around 2 ms).

### Optimization of TRL Imaging Through Circuit Tuning

After all the components in the TRL imager (Fig. 1(D)) were properly assembled, the synchronization between the LED excitation source and the chopper-coupled smartphone camera was elaborately carried out to ensure the maximum S/B ratio for TRL imaging [3].

The optimization strategy of synchronization is that for the chopper driven under a certain frequency saying 250 Hz (2 ms on and 2 ms off in a period), the sum of Pdelay and Pwidth (Pdelay + Pwidth) was fixed at a value (illustrated in Fig. 3(A)). For the fixed sum value, Pwidth was tuned from low to high, and meanwhile, and Pdelay was tuned from high to low. Under each synchronization condition, 100 mg/mL and 0 mg/mL Mn-doped NCs deposited on glass were imaged as signal and background, respectively, and the S/B ratio was calculated. Figure 3 (B–D) show the signal, the background, and their S/B ratio under each testing condition (labeled by the value of Pwidth), when the sum (Pdelay + Pwidth) was set at 440, 880, and 1320 μs, respectively. These three sums are representative values from low to high, in order to examine the effectiveness of our optimization strategy. For each fixed sum, the S/B ratio increases versus the Pwidth and then reach a relative saturation plateau. Moreover, the S/B ratio is enhanced as the sum increases. The maximum S/B ratio (~ 37) was achieved with Pwidth = 1310 μs and Pdelay = 10 μs (the sum = 1320 μs). This is reasonable because a long LED pulse will excite Mn-doped NCs with more energy and the NCs will emit more intense luminescence after LED is turned off. Additionally, with Pwidth = 1310 μs, the delay between LED-off and camera-on is shortest, and thus the camera will catch a stronger signal (the delay is longer as the sum is set at 440 μs or 880 μs, and thus the camera will catch a much-delayed low signal after LED is turned off). Note that with Pdelay = 10 μs, when Pwidth was further increased from 1310 μs to a higher value, the blue UV light from LED was observed to leak into the camera. Thus, Pwidth = 1310 μs and Pdelay = 10 μs is considered as the optimal synchronization condition for 250 Hz. Fig.3 (E) presents the TRL images of 100 μg/mL Mn-doped NCs spotted on glass under different Pwidth values when (Pdelay + Pwidth) is set at 1320 μs. It should be mentioned that the luminescence of the same NC sample under non-time-resolved mode (measuring under continuous excitation) is almost hidden under the autofluorescence from glass and/or sample holder (with a S/B ratio of 1.2, the image not shown).

The same strategy was applied for the chopper driven under different frequencies (i.e., 500 and 1000 Hz). The maximum S/B ratios are ~ 34 and ~ 31 for 500 Hz and 1000 Hz, respectively. Through the comparison among all S/B ratios, Pdelay = 10 μs and Pwidth = 1310 μs under 250 Hz achieved the best S/B ratio and was thus selected as the optimal condition for TRL imaging.

### Anticounterfeiting Application

With the optimal imaging condition, a series of Mn-doped NC solutions with different concentrations were prepared and deposited on glass slides for TRL imaging. Fig. 4(A) shows representative TRL images for different Mn-doped NC concentrations. Fig. 4(B) presents the calibration curve of the TRL intensity of a spot versus the concentration of Mn-doped NCs deposited in the spot. Based on Fig.4(B), the limit of detection (LOD) of Mn-doped NCs is calculated to be around 1.4 μg/mL using the 3-sigma method. Although this low LOD indicates the high sensitivity of the optimized TRL instrument, for the anticounterfeiting application, to save the analysis time and the material cost, a middle-level concentration of Mn-doped NCs with a confidently recognizable intensity by human eye-vision is preferred. Thus, Mn-doped NCs at 50 μg/mL were used in anticounterfeiting application. Fig. 4(C–D) present the imaging of the specific patterns (left and right pointing triangles) of Mn-doped NCs deposited in a 2 × 3 array of wells with undoped NCs as backgrounds. Under continuous excitation (non-time-resolved mode), all wells present orange luminescence and the specific patterns for anticounterfeiting are hidden. Only under TRL measurement, the luminescence of undoped NCs is not measurable due to its short luminescence lifetime (< 1 μs), but the specific patterns from the luminescence of Mn-doped NCs (~ 2 ms luminescence lifetime) can be identified. In this application, the specific patterns in a 2 × 3 array of wells are relatively simple, but we believe that if the ink-printing technology is adopted for NC printing, more complex and dense patterns can be printed to enhance the anticounterfeiting coding information.

## CONCLUSION

In this work, we developed a simple circuit for LED pulsing and timing synchronization, and implemented it in a TRL imager with a UV LED as light source and a chopper-coupled smartphone camera as time-gated optical detector. With circuit-parameter tuning for optimization, the TRL measurement of this imager using this circuit was successfully validated through an anticounterfeiting application using Mn-doped NCs. We believe that this simple circuit can be adopted in the development of point-of-care or in-field TRL measurement instruments for broad applications.

# Positive 2-bridge knots and chirally cosmetic surgeries

**Authors:** Michael Huang ††thanks: University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley, CA. (michael_huang@berkeley.edu) Zelong Li ††thanks: University of California, Los Angeles, Los Angeles, CA. (lizelong831@ucla.edu) Rahi Tanaz ††thanks: University of California, Los Angeles, Los Angeles, CA. (rtanaz@ucla.edu) Chengyi Zhang ††thanks: University of California, Los Angeles, Los Angeles, CA. (chriszhang09@ucla.edu)

## Abstract

In this paper we verify that with the exception of the $(2,2n+1)$ torus knots, positive 2-bridge knots up to 31 crossings do not admit chirally cosmetic surgeries. A knot $K$ admits chirally cosmetic surgeries if there exist surgeries $S^{3}_{r}$ and $S^{3}_{r^{\prime}}$ with distinct slopes $r$ and $r^{\prime}$ such that $S^{3}_{r}(K)\cong-S^{3}_{r^{\prime}}(K)$ , where the negative represents an orientation reversal. To verify this, we use the obstruction formula from [Var21a] which relates classical knot invariants to the existence of chirally cosmetic surgeries. To check the formula, we develop a Python program that computes the classical knot invariants $a_{2}$ , $a_{4}$ , $v_{3}$ , $\det$ , and $g$ of a positive 2-bridge knot.

Keywords: knot theory; cosmetic surgery; Dehn surgery; rational knots

## 1 Introduction

### 1.1 Motivation

Given a knot $K\in S^{3}$ and a slope $r\in\mathbb{Q}\cup\{\infty\}$ , the manifold resulting from Dehn surgery with slope $r$ on $K$ is denoted by $S_{r}^{3}(K)$ . If there exist distinct slopes $r$ and $r^{\prime}$ such that $S_{r}^{3}(K)\cong S_{r^{\prime}}^{3}(K)$ , then the surgeries $S^{3}_{r}$ and $S^{3}_{r^{\prime}}$ are said to be purely cosmetic. If instead $S_{r}^{3}(K)\cong-S_{r^{\prime}}^{3}(K)$ , then the surgeries are said to be chirally cosmetic.

Originally proposed by Bleiler in [Kir95] (Problem 1.81 A), the purely cosmetic surgery conjecture claims that there exist no purely cosmetic surgeries for nontrivial knots in $S^{3}$ . Although this conjecture is still open, there have been many results on special families of knots. It was proved by Ichihara, Jong, Mattman, and Saito that 2-bridge knots admit no purely cosmetic surgeries [Ich+21]. Furthermore, Hanselman has proved the purely cosmetic surgery conjecture for all knots for which each prime summand has 16 or fewer crossings [Han23]. Varvarezos has also shown that 3-braid knots do not admit purely cosmetic surgeries [Var21].

Using machinery from modern Heegaard Floer homology, Varvarezos was also able to construct obstructions to chirally cosmetic surgeries for special families of knots. We use the results from Varvarezos in [Var21a] to prove the non-existence of chirally cosmetic surgeries on positive 2-bridge knots, with the exception of $(2,2n+1)$ torus knots.

### 1.2 Main result

We aim to prove the following result.

#### Theorem 1.1.

Positive 2-bridge knots up to 31 crossings do not admit chirally cosmetic surgeries, with the exception of $(2,2n+1)$ torus knots.

By showing that this result holds for positive 2-bridge knots up to 31 crossings, we will have verified that the conjecture holds for over 1.3 million knots. To prove Theorem 1.1, we will first introduce the background necessary to understand a useful obstruction formula and prove some important theorems and lemmas along the way. We will then describe the Python program we developed in order to calculate the knot invariants used in the obstruction formula, and finally conclude with our results and further directions.

### 1.3 Notation

Let $K$ be a knot. We will use the following notation throughout the paper.

$$ \displaystyle\text{Jones polynomial: }V_{K}(t) \displaystyle\text{Alexander polynomial: }\Delta_{K}(t) \displaystyle\text{Conway polynomial: }\nabla_{K}(z) \displaystyle\text{Conway polynomial coefficients: }\nabla_{K}(z)=a_{0}+a_{2}z^{2}+a_{4}z^{4}+... \displaystyle(p,q)\text{ Rational knot: }C(p,q) \displaystyle\text{Continued fraction: }p/q=a_{1}+\frac{1}{a_{2}+\frac{1}{...+\frac{1}{a_{n}}}}=:[a_{1},a_{2},...,a_{n}] \displaystyle\text{Bridge Number: }Br(K) $$

## 2 Background

### 2.1 Positive 2-bridge knots

In this section, we define the class of positive 2-bridge knots and give a result about continued fraction characterization.

#### Definition 1.

The sign associated to a crossing of the knot K is indicated by Figure 1 below.

*Figure 1: Signed crossings*

A crossing is positive if the understrand is rotated clockwise to match the direction of the overstrand, while a crossing is negative if the understand is rotated counter-clockwise to match the direction of the overstrand.

#### Definition 2.

A knot $K$ is positive if all of its crossings are positive in some projection of $K$ .

#### Definition 3.

The bridge number $Br(K)$ of a knot $K$ is defined to be the minimal number of bridges required in any projection of a $K$ . A bridge in $K$ is an arc which has at least one overcrossing.

#### Remark 2.1.

$Br(K)$ is a knot invariant.

#### Definition 4.

A 2-bridge knot is a knot with $Br(K)=2$ . A positive 2-bridge knot is a 2-bridge knot which is also a positive knot.

As currently defined, the class of positive 2-bridge knots is difficult for a computer program to enumerate, so we seek a more tractable definition.

#### Definition 5.

A tangle in a disk in the plane of projection of a knot $K$ such that $K$ crosses the boundary circle four times. A rational tangle is a tangle that may be unwound into one of the two elementary 2-tangles in Figure 2 by repeatedly twisting the endpoints.

*Figure 2: Elementary 2-tangles*

#### Definition 6.

A rational link is the link that results from closing off the ends of a rational tangle by plait closure. If the resulting link is a knot, it is known as a rational knot.

#### Theorem 2.2 (§3.2, [Ada94]).

The set of 2-bridge knots is identical to the set of rational knots.

Corresponding to the number of twists required before a rotation needed to completely unwind a rational tangle into one of the elementary 2-tangles, we assign a continued fraction decomposition $[a_{1},\dots,a_{n}]$ to a rational knot. We also assign it the rational number $p/q$ that its continued fraction sums to, and hence denote a rational $p/q$ knot $C(p,q)$ . Thus, from Theorem 2.2, we may also characterize 2-bridge knots by a rational number $p/q$ and a continued fraction decomposition $[a_{1},\dots,a_{n}]$ .

#### Theorem 2.3 (Thm. 3.1, [Tan98]).

If a 2-bridge knot $C(p,q),\frac{p}{q}=[a_{1},...,a_{2n+1}]$ satisfies the following conditions:

- i) Each $a_{i}$ is positive

- ii) $a_{i}$ is even if the index is even

then $C(p,q)$ is a positive knot. 11 1 For 2-bridge knots, the strongly quasipositive condition is equivalent to positivity, see [Ozb23] remark 1.5

The converse of Theorem 1 is given in Lemma 2.4 below. With these results we obtain an alternative characterization of 2-bridge knots that is much better suited for a computer program.

#### Lemma 2.4 (Cor. 2.2, [Ozb23]).

If $C(p,q)$ is a positive rational knot, then for some $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ it has a continued fraction decomposition of the form

$$ \displaystyle\frac{p}{q}=a_{1}+\frac{1}{a_{2}+\frac{1}{\ddots+\frac{1}{a_{2n+1}}}} $$

where each $a_{2i}$ is even for $i\in\{1,2,...,n\}$ , and each $a_{i}>0$ .

#### Remark 2.5.

We note that in the paper [Ozb23], the author uses the mirror image of the $C(p,q)$ knot we use. Therefore, their definition of $C(p,p-q)$ is equivalent to our definition of $C(p,q-p)$ . However, due to the results of [KL03], we know that $C(p,q-p)=C(p,q)$ , as $q\equiv q-p\mod{p}$ .

The schematic diagram for a positive 2-bridge knot corresponding to the continued fraction decomposition given in Lemma 2.4 is illustrated in Figure 3 below. The number $a_{i}$ inside each box denotes the number of half twists to be inserted. Note that the figure results in a knot when $\sum_{i=1}^{2n+1}a_{i}$ is odd, while the figure results in a link when $\sum_{i=1}^{2n+1}a_{i}$ is even.

The negative sign on the upper row is due to how half-twists are signed in our notation. Some authors use the opposite notation where instead the bottom row would be negated.

### 2.2 (Chirally) cosmetic surgery

In this section we give a brief overview of Dehn surgery and the cosmetic surgery conjecture. All surgeries unless otherwise specified will be done on the 3-sphere $S^{3}$ .

#### Definition 7.

Given a knot $K$ and a slope $r=\frac{p}{q}\in\mathbb{Q}\cup\{\infty\}$ , Dehn surgery with slope $r$ (often abbreviated $r$ -surgery) on $K$ is the operation of removing a tubular neighborhood of $K\subset S^{3}$ and gluing in a solid torus along the boundary homeomorphism $\phi:T^{2}\rightarrow T^{2}$ , $m\mapsto p\mu+q\lambda$ . The resulting manifold is denoted $S^{3}_{r}(K)$ .

Here, $m$ denotes the meridian on the boundary of the solid torus, $\mu$ denotes the meridian of the tubular neighborhood of $K$ , and $\lambda$ denotes the unique Seifert longitude of $K$ . It is well known that all the self homeomorphisms of $T^{2}$ up to isotopy are given in the form specified in Definition 7.

#### Remark 2.7.

By our convention, $\infty$ -surgery is $\frac{1}{0}$ -surgery. This is the identity since the meridian of the solid torus is glued back to the meridian of the tubular neighborhood, resulting back in our original knot $K\subset S^{3}$ .

We illustrate the idea of of Dehn surgery with slope $r=p/q$ on the trefoil in the Figures 4 and 5 below. For more about Dehn surgery, see [Lic97], [Sav12], [Rol90].

#### Definition 8.

Given a knot $K$ , we say that $K$ admits purely cosmetic surgeries if there exist two distinct slopes $r$ and $r^{\prime}$ such that $S^{3}_{r}(K)\cong S^{3}_{r^{\prime}}(K)$ up to orientation preserving homeomorphism.

#### Conjecture 2.8 (Purely cosmetic surgery conjecture).

No nontrivial knot in $S^{3}$ admits purely cosmetic surgeries.

We consider a related case of this conjecture which we will call the chirally cosmetic surgery conjecture.

#### Definition 9.

A knot $K$ admits chirally cosmetic surgeries if there exist two distinct slopes $r$ and $r^{\prime}$ such that the manifolds resulting from the $r$ and $r^{\prime}$ surgeries are homeomorphic after an orientation reverse, that is, $S^{3}_{r}(K)\cong-S^{3}_{r^{\prime}}(K)$ .

#### Conjecture 2.9 (Chirally cosmetic surgery conjecture).

A knot $K$ does not admit chirally cosmetic surgeries if it is not the unknot, a $(2,2n+1)$ torus knot, or an amphichiral knot.

For an amphichiral knot $K$ , $S^{3}_{r}(K)\cong-S^{3}_{-r}(K)$ . Meanwhile, for $(2,2n+1)$ torus knots, there exist chirally cosmetic surgeries along the slopes $\displaystyle{\tfrac{2n^{2}(2m+1)}{n(2m+1)\pm 1}}$ for each positive integer $m$ (see [IIS21]).

### 2.3 Knot invariants

In this section we introduce relevant knot invariants for the obstruction formula from [Var21a]. We will also provide computationally scalable procedures for retrieving these invariants for positive 2-bridge knots.

#### Definition 10.

The genus ${g(K)}$ of a knot $K$ is the least genus of any Seifert surface for $K$ . A Seifert surface for $K$ is an orientable surface with one boundary component that is the knot $K$ .

#### Lemma 2.10.

Let $K$ be an alternating knot and $\Sigma$ be the Seifert surface obtained from a reduced alternating diagram of $K$ via the Seifert algorithm. Let $s$ be the number of Seifert circles in $\Sigma$ and $c$ be the number of crossings in the alternating diagram. Then, $K$ has genus

$$ g(K)=\frac{1+c-s}{2}. $$

#### Proof.

This result is proved using the Euler characteristic $\chi$ of $\Sigma$ . Notice that any Seifert surface of a knot $K$ can be deformation retracted to be a graph with a vertex at each Seifert circle and an edge at each crossing. The Euler characteristic of $\Sigma$ is then given by the number of vertices minus the number of edges plus $1$ , since there are two faces but we have one boundary component with boundary $K$ . By definition, $\displaystyle{g=\tfrac{2-\chi}{2}}$ and we have $\chi=s-c+1$ , thus we get $\displaystyle{g(K)\leq\tfrac{1+c-s}{2}}$ . It is well-known that the Seifert algorithm when applied to a reduced alternating projection of a link yields a minimal genus Seifert surface (see [Gab86]), so we are done. ∎

With Lemma 2.10, we have a closed-form description of the genus of a positive 2-bridge knot.

#### Lemma 2.11.

If $K=C(p,q)$ has the continued fraction decomposition $[a_{1},...,a_{2n+1}]$ satisfying Lemma 2.4. above, then $K$ has genus

$$ \displaystyle g(K)=\frac{1}{2}\left(\sum\limits_{i=0}^{n}a_{2i+1}-1\right) $$

#### Proof.

Consider the standard projection of a positive 2-bridge knot as in Figure 3, we give the projection an orientation as in Figure 7. We will apply the Seifert algorithm to obtain the Seifert surface of $K$ (note that all positive 2-bridge knot diagrams are alternating). First, we will take the oriented resolution (see Figure 6) at each crossing to obtain Figure 8. Next, we add half-twisted bands in the place of where each crossing used to be, obtaining Figure 9. Now, we can count the number of crossings and Seifert circles to get the genus from Lemma 2.10. Clearly, $c=\sum_{i=1}^{2n+1}a_{i}$ . For $s$ , we can notice that each upper strand (corresponding to the $a_{2i}$ ) contributes $a_{2i}-1$ circles, and each lower strand $a_{2i+1}$ contributes only one circle. We group the circle from each lower strand to the next upper strand, with the exception of the last lower strand. This gives $s=\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{2i}+1+1$ where we have an extra circle from the big circle in the background. Plugging these values in, we get the desired formula. ∎

*Figure 6: Oriented resolution of a crossing*

*Figure 8: Resolving crossings and resulting Seifert circles*

#### Lemma 2.12 (Section 4, [IW19]).

If $K=C(p,q)$ is a positive two bridge knot with $|p|>|q|$ , then there exist $p^{\prime},q^{\prime}\in\mathbb{Z}$ such that $C(p^{\prime},q^{\prime})=C(p,q)$ and $\frac{p^{\prime}}{q^{\prime}}$ has an even continued fraction representation of the form

$$ \frac{p^{\prime}}{q^{\prime}}=a_{1}+\frac{1}{a_{2}+\frac{1}{\ddots+\frac{1}{a_{2n}}}} $$

where $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and each of $a_{i}\neq 0$ is even for $i\in\mathbb{N}$ . $p^{\prime},q^{\prime}$ can be obtained with the following conditions:

- 1. $(p^{\prime},q^{\prime})=(p,q)$ if $q$ is even

- 2. if $q$ is odd, $p^{\prime}=p$ and $q^{\prime}=q\pm p$ with the restriction that $|q^{\prime}|<|p^{\prime}|$ .

#### Proof.

To prove this lemma, we assume that we already have the construction that $|p|>|q|$ with $q$ even. We apply induction on $|q|$ .

Base case: if $|q|=2$ , then we have $q=\pm 2$ , then because we have $|p|>|q|$ and $p$ , $q$ coprime, we must have $\frac{p}{q}=a_{1}\pm\frac{1}{2}$ , with $a_{1}=\lfloor(p/q)\rfloor$ if $\lfloor(p/q)\rfloor$ even, and $a_{1}=\lfloor(p/q)\rfloor+1$ otherwise. Since we have $|p|>|q|$ , we cannot have $a_{1}=0$ , which satisfies the conditions of a even continued fraction defined in the theorem.

For the inductive step, we suppose that the even continued fraction exists for all such $p,q^{\prime}$ with $|q^{\prime}|\leq 2n$ . Let’s consider $p,q$ with $q=2(n+1)$ . Then we rewrite $p=q+h$ , where $h\in\mathbb{Z}$ . Now we set $a_{1}$ as the even number in $\lfloor(p/q)\rfloor$ and $\lfloor(p/q)\rfloor+1$ , then we can rewrite

$$ \frac{q+h}{q}=a_{1}-(a_{1}-\frac{q+h}{q}) $$

$$ \frac{q+h}{q}=a_{1}-\frac{1}{\frac{q}{(a_{1}-1)q-h}} $$

It is crucial to realize that due to the choice of $a_{1}$ , we have ensured that $|q|>|(a_{1}-1)q-h|$ . Denote $q_{1}=(a_{1}-1)q-h$ . Also, because $q$ is even and $h$ is odd, we must have $q_{1}$ odd. Then we apply a similar procedure on $\frac{q}{(a_{1}-1)q-h}$ . We have

$$ \frac{q+h}{q}=a_{1}-\frac{1}{\frac{q}{q_{1}}}=a_{1}-\frac{1}{a_{2}-\frac{a_{2}q_{1}-q}{q_{1}}}=a_{1}-\frac{1}{a_{2}-\frac{1}{\frac{q_{1}}{a_{2}q_{1}-q}}} $$

At this stage, if $a_{2}q_{1}-q=0$ , then we are done. If otherwise, once again, we must have $|q_{1}|>|a_{2}q_{1}-q|$ , and also because $q_{1}$ odd, $a_{2}$ even, and q even, we have $a_{2}q_{1}-q$ even. Then remember that $|q|>|q_{1}|>|a_{2}q_{1}-q|$ . Then by the inductive hypothesis, $\frac{q_{1}}{a_{2}q_{1}-q}$ has an even continued fraction. Thus $\frac{p}{q}$ has an even continued fraction. ∎

With this even continued fraction decomposition, we have another alternative way to obtain the genus of a positive 2-bridge knot.

#### Theorem 2.13 (§4, [IW19]).

If K = C(p,q) and $K$ has the even continued fraction representation $[2b_{1},2c_{1},\dots,2b_{n},2c_{n}]$ as constructed in Lemma 2.12, then $g(K)=n$ , where $n$ is half the length of the even continued fraction representation.

#### Definition 11.

The Jones polynomial of any link $L$ can be characterized by the following skein relation:

$$ t^{-1}V(L_{+})-tV(L_{-})+(t^{-1/2}-t^{1/2})V(L_{0})=0 $$

where $L_{-},L_{+}$ , and $L_{0}$ represents the three ways of resolving a particular crossing for $L$ (see Figure 10). We normalize $V(U)=1$ , where $U$ is the unknot.

*Figure 10: $L_{+}$ , $L_{-}$ , and $L_{0}$*

#### Theorem 2.14 (Proposition 4.4, [IW19]).

If $K=C(p,q)$ and $K$ has the even continued fraction representation $[2b_{1},2c_{1},\dots,2b_{n},2c_{n}]$ as constructed in Lemma 2.12, then we can calculate knot invariant $v_{3}$ as below.

$$ v_{3}(K)=\frac{1}{2}\left(\sum\limits_{k=1}^{n}c_{k}(\sum\limits_{i=1}^{k}b_{i})^{2}-\sum\limits_{k=1}^{n}b_{k}(\sum\limits_{i=k}^{n}c_{i})^{2}\right) $$

Alternatively, we can calculate $v_{3}$ directly from the Jones polynomial with the following formula.

$$ v_{3}(K)=-\frac{1}{36}V_{K}^{\prime\prime\prime}(1)-\frac{1}{12}V_{K}^{\prime\prime}(1). $$

In Section 3, we explain that our program always verifies that $v_{3}\neq 0$ before checking the obstruction formula given in Corollary 2.18.

#### Definition 12.

The Alexander polynomial of any link $L$ can be characterized by the following skein relation:

$$ \Delta(L_{+})-\Delta(L_{-})=(t^{1/2}-t^{-1/2})\Delta(L_{0}) $$

with $\Delta(U)=1$ , where $U$ is the unknot. One can then find the Conway polynomial of any link L by making the substitution $\Delta_{L}(t^{2})=\nabla_{L}(t-t^{-1})$ . The skein relation follows accordingly:

$$ \nabla(L_{+})-\nabla(L_{-})=z\nabla(L_{0}). $$

See Figure 10 for $L_{+}$ , $L_{-}$ , and $L_{0}$ .

For an alternative way to calculate the Alexander polynomial, see Appendix 6.1. Due to the higher time complexity of calculating determinants of large matrices, the recursive relation was chosen to be implemented in the code.

From the Conway polynomial, we can extract a few more important invariants.

#### Definition 13.

The $a_{2}$ and $a_{4}$ invariants of a knot $K$ are the coefficients of the $z^{2}$ and $z^{4}$ terms respectively in $\nabla_{K}(z)$ .

#### Definition 14.

The determinant of a knot is given by

$$ \det(K)=|\Delta_{K}(-1)|=|\nabla_{K}(2i)| $$

Equivalently, we can get the determinant of $K$ as the absolute value of substituting $z^{2}=-4$ in $\nabla_{K}(z)$ .

### 2.4 Obstruction formula

In this section, we will derive an obstruction formula to the existence of chirally cosmetic surgeries which follows the work Vavarezos in [Var21a]. Although the actual content of some of these formulas requires background in Heegaard Floer homology, we can state the main results without issue.

#### Theorem 2.15 (2.8, [Var21a]).

Let $K$ be knot satisfying $\tau(K)=g(K)$ , and $v_{3}(K)\neq 0$ . If $S_{p/q}^{3}(K)\cong-S_{p/q^{\prime}}^{3}(K)$ for some $p,q>0,q^{\prime}<0$ then

$$ v_{3}(K)(Vert(K)+2g(K)-1)=7a_{2}(K)^{2}-a_{2}(K)-10a_{4}(K) $$

$Vert(K)$ and $\tau(K)$ are modern knot invariants derived from Heegaard Floer homology, but as they are not used in the final form of the obstruction formula, we will not discuss them further. See [OS06] and [Man16] for precise definitions.

#### Remark 2.16.

Notice that in Theorem 2.15 we are only considering the cases of $p,q>0,$ $q^{\prime}<0$ . This is because for any non- $L$ -space22 2 An $L$ -space knot is a knot $K$ such that $S^{3}_{r}(K)$ is an $L$ -space for some $r\in\mathbb{Q}_{+}$ . For more details, see [OS03]. knot K, if $S_{r}^{3}(K)=\pm S_{r^{\prime}}^{3}(K)$ , then $r,r^{\prime}$ must have different signs [Var21a].

#### Lemma 2.17 (3.5, [Var21a]).

If K is an alternating knot with $\tau(K)>0$ , then

$$ Vert(K)=\frac{1}{2}\det(K)+\tau(K)-\frac{3}{2} $$

We now have the necessary tools to modify the obstruction formula given in Theorem 2.15 to only include the classical knot invariants discussed in Section 2.3. The resulting formula given in Corollary 2.18 below is the final version of the obstruction formula we will use in our program.

#### Corollary 2.18.

Let $K$ be a a positive 2-bridge knot which is also not a $(2,2n+1)$ -torus knot. If $K$ admits a chirally cosmetic surgery, then

$$ v_{3}\left(\frac{1}{2}\det(K)+3g-\frac{5}{2}\right)=7a_{2}^{2}-a_{2}-10a_{4} $$

#### Proof.

We first show that positive 2-bridge knots satisfy the conditions necessary for Theorem 2.15 and Lemma 2.17. From 1.8 in [Hed10], we see that positive knots satisfy $\tau(K)=g(K)$ . For knots with a positive diagram with $c$ crossings, we have $v_{3}(K)>c$ from [Sto03]. Since the unknot does not have two bridges, we have that $v_{3}(K)\neq 0$ for any positive two bridge knots. Next, from [OS05], we know that the only rational knots which are also L-space knots are exactly those which are $(2,2n+1)-$ torus knots, so upon excluding this subfamily, the condition for Lemma 2.17 is also satisfied. The result is then immediate when substituting Lemma 2.17 into Theorem 2.15. ∎

We are interested in the contrapositive of Corollary 2.18, which is given in Corollary 2.19 below.

#### Corollary 2.19.

Let $K$ be a knot as in Corollary 2.18 and with up to 31 crossings. If $K$ satisfies

$$ \displaystyle v_{3}\left(\frac{1}{2}\det(K)+3g-\frac{5}{2}\right)\neq 7a_{2}^{2}-a_{2}-10a_{4} $$

from Theorem 2.18, then $K$ does not admit chirally cosmetic surgeries.

## 3 Python code

In this section we provide a brief overview of the Python implementation we used for validating the main result by checking the obstruction formula in Corollary 2.19. For code resources, consult https://github.com/zl830/chiral_cosmetic_surgery_for_pos_2_bridge_knots.

### 3.1 High level overview

The code can be summarized as follows:

- 1. Input a maximum number of crossings.

- 2. Generate every possible positive 2-bridge knot up to said maximum number of crossings. Each knot is represented as a list $[a_{1},...,a_{m}]$ which corresponds to the continued fraction of $p/q$ .

- 3. For each presentation of a knot, calculate the Conway polynomial via a recursive skein relation to get $a_{2}$ and $a_{4}$ .

- 4. Calculate the determinant of the knot by substituting $z^{2}=-4$ in the Conway polynomial.

- 5. Find the even continued fraction representation to get genus and $v_{3}$ .

- 6. Check if the obstruction formula is satisfied.

- 7. Loop through each knot up to maximum number of crossings.

### 3.2 Skein relation recursion

To compute the Conway polynomial, recall that a positive two-bridge knot can be arranged as in Figure 3. We untangle the knot by resolving the crossings from left to right, and use the skein relation from Definition 12 to compute the polynomial. At each step, we have the following cases to consider:

- 1. The leftmost braid is $a_{i}$ where $i$ is odd and $a_{i}\geq 3$ . The resolutions give the links corresponding to $[a_{i}-2,a_{i+1},\dots,a_{2n+1}]$ and $[a_{i}-1,a_{i+1},\dots,a_{2n+1}]$ for $L_{-}$ and $L_{0}$ respectively. Figure 11: Case 1

- 2. The leftmost braid is $a_{i}$ where $i$ is odd and $a_{i}=2$ . The resolutions give the links corresponding to $[0,a_{i+1},\dots,a_{2n+1}]$ and $[1,a_{i+1},\dots,a_{2n+1}]$ for $L_{-}$ and $L_{0}$ respectively. In the former case, we can simply untwist the next braid, so we reduce to $[a_{i+2},\dots,a_{2n+1}]$ . In the latter case, we have $[a_{i+1}+1,a_{i+2},\dots,a_{2n+1}]$ . This process is depicted in Figures 12 and 13. Figure 12: Case 2 Figure 13: Case 2 reduced

- 3. The leftmost braid is $a_{i}$ where $i$ is odd and $a_{i}=1$ or $a_{i}=0$ . We use the same reduction in case 2, illustrated in Figure 13.

- 4. The leftmost braid is $a_{i}$ where $i$ is even. Notice that from the above process and the fact that $a_{i}$ is even if $i$ is even for a positive two-bridge knot (Lemma 2.4), we have the resolutions in Figure 14. $L_{-}$ is the link corresponding to $[a_{i}-2,a_{i+1},\dots,a_{2n+1}]$ . $L_{0}$ can be further untwisted and we are left with $[a_{i+1},\dots,a_{2n+1}]$ . Figure 14: Case 4

- 5. Resolving the even braids as in case 4 will result in the case where the leftmost braid is $a_{i}$ where $i$ is even and $a_{i}=1$ . However, this twist can be simply incorporated into the next braid, resulting in $[a_{i+1}+1,a_{i+2},\dots,a_{2n+1}]$ , as shown in Figure 15 Figure 15: Case 5

At the end of this process, we are left with either the unknot, or the trivial link with two components. These have Conway polynomial $1$ and $0$ respectively.

## 4 Results

### 4.1 Proof of main result

We now obtain the main result given in Theorem 1.1:

#### Theorem 4.1.

Positive 2-bridge knots with up to 31 crossings do not admit chirally cosmetic surgeries, with the exception of $(2,2n+1)$ torus knots.

#### Proof.

This theorem was verified computationally by running the aforementioned python program for all positive 2-bridge knots up to 31 crossings. No knot resulted in an equality of the obstruction formula. The result thus directly follows from Corollary 2.19. ∎

#### Remark 4.2.

In theory, the program can verify knots up to any specified number of crossings, but the memory and time complexity scales exponentially with the number of crossings.

The 31 crossing threshold was picked because this number allowed us to verify over a million knots, 1,346,268 to be exact. To expedite the recursive process, we used a dynamic database to store the links that were the results of resolutions from the skein relation, for use in more complicated links. Even for such a relatively small number, the program took 100 minutes to complete and used around 8GB of RAM (memory). We have included the values returned (namely the rational number $p/q$ , the left-hand side and the right-hand side of obstruction formula 2.18, and whether the formula is an equality) in Appendix 6.2.

### 4.2 Future directions and further results

Although we did not verify the conjecture explicitly for all positive 2-bridge knots, the result of this paper could lead to future work towards the larger result. One possible direction would be proving the general case of inequality in the obstruction formula through an inductive argument. As explained in the skein relation recursion, each positive 2-bridge knot can be simplified into two 2-bridge knots with strictly fewer crossings. Using these resolutions, there may exist a strict inequality involving the sides of the obstruction formula 2.18 which could be stated in terms of crossing number or continued fraction representation. If such an inequality exists, the Conjecture 2.9 would be proved for all positive 2-bridge knots.

#### Remark 4.3.

In most of the cases our program checked, the left-hand side of the obstruction formula was larger than the right-hand side. The right-hand side is larger when the knot is a $(2,2n+1)$ torus knot and when both $p$ and $q$ are relatively small.

In light of this observation, we created a plot to compare the complexity of the knot $C(p,q)$ to the quotient obtained from dividing the absolute values of the left-hand side of the obstruction formula by the right-hand side. The $\mathcal{L}^{1}$ norm was was chosen to measure complexity, and

$$ \displaystyle|p|+|q| $$

was plotted against

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\left|v_{3}\left(\frac{1}{2}\det(K)+3g-\frac{5}{2}\right)\right|}{\left|7a_{2}^{2}-a_{2}-10a_{4}\right|} $$

for each positive knot $C(p,q)$ up to 17 crossings. The resulting plot is shown in Figure 16. Additional plots comparing different measures of complexity against different forms derived from the obstruction formula are included in Appendix 6.3.

*Figure 16: Plot of knot complexity vs. obstruction formula quotient for positive 2-bridge knots up to 17 crossings*

As apparent in Figure 16, the general trend is that the quotient given in (2) increases as the complexity of the knot $C(p,q)$ given by (1) increases, and similar results hold for the plots given in Appendix 6.3 as well. For $|p|+|q|$ sufficiently large, we also note that since by Remark 4.3 the numerator of (2) is known to always be strictly greater than the denominator of (2) for positive knots $C(p,q)$ up to 17 crossings, the expression given in (2) is always strictly greater than 1 for the plot given in Figure 16.

If we disregard the cases where $p$ and $q$ are small, these results suggest that for even higher complexity positive 2-bridge knots such as those exceeding 31 crossings, the expression given in (2) will likely continue to be strictly greater than 1. In fact, the trend in the plot from Figure 16 suggests that higher complexity knots will result in values of (2) which are actually much greater than 1. This in turn would indicate that the left-hand side of the obstruction formula is always strictly greater than the right-hand side and thus that the obstruction formula never results in equality for any positive 2-bridge knot with the exception of the $(2,2n+1)$ torus knots. These ideas lead us to the following conjectures.

#### Conjecture 4.4.

If $K$ is a positive 2-bridge knot, with rational number $p/q$ satisfying $p,q>20$ , then

$$ v_{3}\left(\frac{1}{2}\det(K)+3g-\frac{5}{2}\right)>7a_{2}^{2}-a_{2}-10a_{4} $$

If Conjecture 4.4 is shown to be true, then Conjecture 4.5 below follows immediately from Corollary 2.19, along with a separate proof for knots of lower complexity (with small $p$ and $q$ ).

#### Conjecture 4.5.

Positive 2-bridge knots do not admit chirally cosmetic surgeries, with the exception of $(2,2n+1)$ torus knots.

## 6 Appendix

### 6.1 Seifert Form

In this section, we give an alternative way to calculate the Alexander (and thus Conway) polynomial of a positive 2-bridge knot.

Recall that we can get the Seifert matrix (or form) $S$ of a knot $K$ by the $n\times n$ matrix of integers $S_{ij}=\text{lk}(x_{i},x_{j}^{+})$ . Here, the $x_{i}$ are the generators of $H_{1}(S^{3}\setminus K)$ , $x_{i}^{+}$ is the positive pushoff of $x_{i}$ , and lk is the linking number. This matrix can be written out explicitly for positive 2-bridge knots in the following form.

#### Theorem 6.1.

Given a continued fraction representation consistent with Lemma 2.4, we can write the Seifert form in the following block diagonal form.

$$ S=\begin{pmatrix}A_{1}&0&\cdots&\cdots&0\\
1&-1-\frac{a_{2}}{2}&0&\cdots&0\\
0&1&A_{3}&\cdots&\vdots\\
\vdots&\ddots&\ddots&\ddots&0\\
0&\cdots&0&1&A_{2n+1}\end{pmatrix} $$

with $a_{i}-1\times a_{i}-1$ blocks

$$ A_{i}=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0&\cdots&&0\\
1&-1&\ddots&&0\\
0&\ddots&\ddots&&\vdots\\
\vdots&\ddots&\ddots&\ddots&0\\
0&\cdots&0&1&-1\end{pmatrix}. $$

#### Proof.

This result can be seen by considering a projection of the type in Figure 3 and explicitly calculating linking numbers. ∎

With the Seifert form for $K$ , we can directly get the Alexander polynomial $\Delta_{K}(t)=\det\left(tS-S^{T}\right)$ .
